name: Beaux-Arts
summary: A grand classical system taught at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris: a clear plan on axes, a rich sculpted front with paired columns and a mansard roof. It made the opera house, the station and the city hall into public palaces.

philosophy.core_thesis: A great building is planned first: the parti is a clear sequence of axes, rooms and routes, and classical ornament and sculpture crown the plan.
design_principles: Start from the plan: a main axis, one or two cross axes, and rooms in a hierarchy of size from the entrance hall to the grand salon.
Compose the front as a symmetric tripartite order: a base, a colonnade or giant order, and an attic or mansard roof.
Mark the central pavilion and the end pavilions by projecting 0.5 to 2m and by a higher roof.
Use paired columns and a rich classical entablature on the main storey, with sculpture groups on the attic.
Make a grand stair or hall of 15 to 25m height as the climax of the plan, in marble and gilding.
Join the building to the city: a front on a square or an avenue, with the axis continued by the street.
anti_patterns: Plans without an axis or a clear hierarchy of rooms
Bare undecorated walls and flat roofs without sculpture
Exposed steel frames and visible industrial structure on the front
Gothic or Romanesque motifs in the main order
Small, modest rooms in the main sequence

massing.form: A symmetric block with a central pavilion, end pavilions and a long colonnade between, on a raised base.
massing.proportion: A front of 3:1 to 5:1; the central pavilion is 1.3 to 1.6 times the height of the wings.
massing.roof: A mansard roof in slate or copper with sculpted dormers, or a low dome over the central hall, and a balustrade with statues.
massing.relation_to_ground: A rusticated base of one storey, a wide flight of steps, and a forecourt on the axis of an avenue.

structure.system: A steel or iron frame with a stone cladding, or load-bearing masonry; the orders and the sculpture are stone.
structure.span_and_module: Bays of 4.5 to 6m; the central hall spans 18 to 30m; the storey height of the piano nobile is 5 to 8m.
structure.expression: The frame is hidden under the stone; the orders state the order of the plan, not the load.

materials.finish: Polished and carved: pale cut stone with rich marble, bronze and gilding inside.

facade.composition: A symmetric front in three vertical tiers and three horizontal parts, with central and end pavilions, and sculpture groups.
facade.openings: Tall round-headed arches on the base, tall pedimented windows on the main floor; the window-to-wall ratio is 20 to 35%.

light_and_space.daylight: Light enters from roof-lights and tall windows; the grand hall is lit from above by a glass dome.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A planned sequence on the axis: vestibule, grand stair, foyer, then the main hall; the cross axis links the side halls.
light_and_space.interior_character: Marble stairs, gilded balustrades, painted ceilings, sculpture in niches and a mosaic floor.

ornament.attitude: Ornament is a rich public language: classical orders, sculpture and allegory tell the city what the building is for.

rules.rule: Plan on a main axis and a cross axis, and continue the axis into the street.
Rank rooms by size from the vestibule to the grand salon.
Group the public halls on the piano nobile and the services below and behind.
Lead the visitor along the axis by a grand stair to the main hall.
Group the front in a central pavilion and two end pavilions with a colonnade between.
End the axis in the great hall under a glass dome.

images.title: Façade of the Opéra Garnier, Paris

emotion.target_response: Civic pride and grandeur: the viewer feels that the city offers a palace to every citizen.

avoid_when: The brief asks for a minimal, modern or low-key building.
The plan has no room for a main axis and a grand hall.

modifiers.how: Strip the mansard, the sculpture groups and the paired columns; keep the symmetry, the portico and the pale stone.

canonical_works.architect: John L. Smithmeyer and Paul J. Pelz
Reed and Stem; Warren and Wetmore

sources.title: Arthur Drexler (ed.), The Architecture of the École des Beaux-Arts (Museum of Modern Art, 1977)
